In [[algebraic topology]], the '''pushforward''' of a [[continuous function]] <math>f</math> : <math>X \rightarrow Y</math> between two [[topological space]]s is a [[homomorphism]]  <math>f_{*}:H_n\left(X\right) \rightarrow H_n\left(Y\right)</math> between the [[homology group]]s for <math>n \geq 0</math>.

Homology is a [[functor]] which converts a topological space <math>X</math> into a sequence of homology groups <math>H_{n}\left(X\right)</math>. (Often, the collection of all such groups is referred to using the notation <math>H_{*}\left(X\right)</math>; this collection has the structure of a [[graded ring]].) In any [[category (mathematics)|category]], a functor must induce a corresponding [[morphism]]. The pushforward is the morphism corresponding to the homology functor.

== Definition for singular and simplicial homology ==

We build the pushforward homomorphism as follows (for [[singular homology|singular]] or [[simplicial homology]]):

First, the map <math>f\colon X\to Y</math> induces a homomorphism between the singular or simplicial [[chain complex]]   <math>C_n\left(X\right)</math> and <math>C_n\left(Y\right)</math> defined by composing each singular n-[[simplex]] <math>\sigma_X\colon\Delta^n\rightarrow X</math> with <math>f</math> to obtain a singular n-simplex of <math>Y</math>, <math>f_{\#}\left(\sigma_X\right) = f\sigma_X\colon\Delta^n\rightarrow Y</math>, and extending this linearly via <math>f_{\#}\left(\sum_tn_t\sigma_t\right) = \sum_tn_tf_{\#}\left(\sigma_t\right)</math>.

The maps <math>f_{\#}\colon C_n\left(X\right)\rightarrow C_n\left(Y\right)</math> satisfy <math>f_{\#}\partial = \partial f_{\#}</math> where <math>\partial</math> is the [[boundary operator]] between chain groups, so <math>\partial f_{\#}</math> defines a [[chain complex#Chain maps|chain map]].
<!-- We have a diagram
<math>
\[
\begin{array}{ccccccccc}
\dots & \rightarrow & C_{n+1}\left(X\right) & \overset{\partial}{\rightarrow} & C_{n}\left(X\right) & \overset{\partial}{\rightarrow} & C_{n-1}\left(X\right) & \rightarrow & \dots\\
 &  & \downarrow{\scriptstyle f_{\#}} &  & \downarrow{\scriptstyle f_{\#}} &  & \downarrow{\scriptstyle f_{\#}}\\
\dots & \rightarrow & C_{n+1}\left(Y\right) & \overset{\partial}{\rightarrow} & C_{n}\left(Y\right) & \overset{\partial}{\rightarrow} & C_{n-1}\left(Y\right) & \rightarrow & \dots\end{array}\]
</math> 
such that in each square <math>f_{\#}\partial = \partial f_{\#}</math>, so <math>\partial f_{\#}</math> defines a '''chain map'''.
-->

Therefore, <math>f_{\#}</math> takes cycles to cycles, since <math>\partial \alpha = 0</math> implies <math>\partial f_{\#}\left( \alpha \right) = f_{\#}\left(\partial \alpha \right) = 0</math>. Also <math>f_{\#}</math> takes boundaries to boundaries since <math> f_{\#}\left(\partial \beta \right) = \partial f_{\#}\left(\beta \right)</math>.

Hence <math>f_{\#}</math> induces a homomorphism between the homology groups <math>f_{*} : H_n\left(X\right) \rightarrow H_n\left(Y\right)</math> for <math>n\geq0</math>.

== Properties and homotopy invariance ==

{{Main|Singular homology#Homotopy invariance}}

Two basic properties of the push-forward are:

# <math>\left( f\circ g\right)_{*} = f_{*}\circ g_{*}</math> for the composition of maps <math>X\overset{g}{\rightarrow}Y\overset{f}{\rightarrow}Z</math>.
# <math>\left( \text{id}_X \right)_{*} = \text{id}</math> where <math>\text{id}_X</math> : <math>X\rightarrow X</math> refers to identity function of <math>X</math> and  <math>\text{id}\colon H_n\left(X\right) \rightarrow H_n\left(X\right)</math> refers to the identity isomorphism of homology groups.

(This shows the [[functor]]iality of the pushforward.)

A main result about the push-forward is the '''homotopy invariance''': if two maps <math>f,g\colon X\rightarrow Y</math> are [[homotopic]], then they induce the same homomorphism <math>f_{*} = g_{*}\colon H_n\left(X\right) \rightarrow H_n\left(Y\right)</math>.

This immediately implies (by the above properties) that the homology groups of homotopy equivalent spaces are isomorphic: The maps <math>f_{*}\colon H_n\left(X\right) \rightarrow H_n\left(Y\right)</math> induced by a homotopy equivalence <math>f\colon X\rightarrow Y</math> are isomorphisms for all <math>n</math>.
